unit.title: Doubles Strategy
unit.summary: Position on the court, the third-shot drop, moving as a team, middle-ball calls, stacking, switching, poaching and targeting.

lessons.title: Two up, two back
lessons.objective: Explain the standard court positions in doubles.

payload.prompt: Tap the two-up formation.

diagram.alt: Doubles court from above with the two-up formation highlighted

explanation.correct: Two-up is the ideal position: both partners at the kitchen line, ready to volley and control.
explanation.incorrect: Two-up means both at the kitchen line, not spread out or at the baseline.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two up means both partners at the net, the winning formation.

payload.prompt: Why is 'two-up' the ideal formation in doubles?

options.text: It lets both partners control the net and volley down at the opponents
It's easier to run from the baseline
It gives you more space to hit drives
It's called that because there are two players

explanation.correct: Two-up wins because you're at the net, ready to volley and put pressure on the opponents.
explanation.incorrect: Two-up is powerful because of net control and the ability to volley. It's not about spacing or baseline mobility.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-up: both at the net, controlling the rally.

payload.prompt: Match each court position to its description.

pairs.definition: Both partners at the kitchen line, the winning formation in doubles.
Both partners at the baseline, the starting position when receiving a serve.
One player at the net and one at the baseline, the in-between phase.

distractorDefinitions: Both players at the service line

explanation.summary: Court positioning evolves: you start two-back on the return, move through transition, and aim for two-up to control.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-back at start, transition as you move, two-up to win.

payload.prompt: Complete the positioning strategy.
payload.template: In doubles, {{formation}} is the goal because both players can {{control-action}}.

explanation.correct: Two-up is the winning formation; at the net you can volley and take control of each rally.
explanation.incorrect: The goal is two-up at the kitchen line, where both partners can volley and take control.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-up wins because you're in control.

payload.prompt: After the serve and return, your team is at the baseline for the third shot. Which is the smart play?

options.text: A soft drop into the kitchen so you have time to advance to the net
A hard drive to end the point immediately
A lob to get them away from the net
Any shot, it doesn't matter

explanation.correct: The third-shot drop is the foundation of doubles strategy: soft arc into the kitchen buys time for your team to move up.
explanation.incorrect: The third shot is usually a soft drop, not a drive. Drives are risky when you're at the baseline.
explanation.sayThisLine: Third shot: soft drop to buy time, then move up.

payload.prompt: You're at the baseline after the return. Your opponent's third shot is coming. Do you attack it or prepare to move up?

situation.narrative: The other team is hitting their third shot from the baseline. It could be a drop or a drive.

facts.label: Your goal
facts.value: Get to the net without getting hit

options.label: Prepare to advance; assume it's a soft drop
options.consequence: Smart. Most teams hit a soft drop on the third shot, giving you time to move to the kitchen line.
considerations: Soft drops are the dominant third-shot choice
You have time to move up

options.label: Attack immediately, assume it's weak
options.consequence: Risky. Most third shots are soft drops that you cannot attack from the baseline.
considerations: A hard drive from baseline can hurt

payload.expertNote: On the third shot, assume a soft drop and move up. If they surprise with a drive, back up and be ready.

payload.prompt: Your team hits a hard, aggressive third shot at their feet. Is this a standard third-shot strategy?

scene.alt: Third-shot scenario: hard aggressive shot from the baseline.

explanation.correct: A hard third-shot drive is risky when you're at the baseline and they're at the net. The drop is the standard play.
explanation.incorrect: The third-shot drop is the standard; a drive is possible but riskier because you're back and they may be closer to the net.
explanation.sayThisLine: Third shot: drop is standard, drive is a risky gamble.

payload.prompt: Complete the third-shot strategy.
payload.template: The {{shot-type}} is the standard third shot because it {{reason}} while a {{alternative}} is riskier.

explanation.correct: The drop is the standard because it gives your team time to move to the net, the winning position.
explanation.incorrect: Drop is standard; it buys time. Drive is the alternative choice.
explanation.sayThisLine: Drop buys time, drive is a gamble.

lessons.title: Drop it, then move up
lessons.objective: Understand why the drop buys time to reach the line.

payload.prompt: A soft third-shot drop lands in the kitchen. Your team now has time to advance. True?

scene.alt: Third-shot scenario: soft drop in the kitchen, team has time to move.

choices.label: True, the drop buys us time
False, we still have to hurry

explanation.correct: The soft drop lands in the kitchen and takes time to get there, giving your team a moment to advance from the baseline.
explanation.incorrect: A soft drop into the kitchen does buy time; it's why it's the standard third shot.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft drop buys time; advance while they're away from net.

payload.prompt: As you advance from the baseline to the kitchen line after a drop, which zone are you crossing?

options.text: The transition zone (no-man's-land), where you're vulnerable if a ball is hit hard
The service box
The kitchen
The boundary zone

explanation.correct: The transition zone is mid-court, the riskiest area. That's why the drop buys time: to cross it safely.
explanation.incorrect: The transition zone (mid-court between baseline and kitchen line) is what you must cross after a soft drop.
explanation.sayThisLine: Crossing the transition zone after a soft drop gives you time.

payload.prompt: Complete the third-shot drop strategy.
payload.template: The {{shot-type}} lands in the kitchen and {{what-happens}}, so your team has time to {{action}}.

explanation.correct: The drop takes time, giving your team a window to advance from baseline to the kitchen line.
explanation.incorrect: Drop into kitchen gives time; use that moment to advance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft drop buys time to advance to the net.

lessons.title: The transition zone
lessons.objective: Identify no-man's-land and how to cross it.

payload.prompt: Tap the transition zone.

explanation.correct: The transition zone is the risky mid-court area between baseline and kitchen line. The soft drop buys time to cross it safely.
explanation.incorrect: The transition zone is mid-court, where a fast ball can catch you off-guard.
explanation.sayThisLine: Transition zone is no-man's land; cross it quickly after a soft drop.

payload.prompt: Put the steps for safely crossing the transition zone in order.

items.text: Hit a soft third-shot drop that lands in the kitchen
items.why: This gives the opponents time to respond and gives you time to advance.

items.text: Start moving forward from the baseline while the ball is in flight
items.why: The drop is already in the air, so you begin your advance immediately.

items.text: Cross the transition zone (mid-court) while staying alert
items.why: Move through the risky area quickly but controlled.

items.text: Split-step and get to the kitchen line in ready position
items.why: Prepare for the opponent's next shot with a split-step as they hit.

items.text: You're now at the kitchen line with control of the point
items.why: Two-up formation achieved; you're in the winning position.

explanation.correct: The sequence is drop-advance-cross-ready-control. Each step builds on the last.
explanation.incorrect: Start with the soft drop, then advance through the transition zone, and finish ready at the net.
explanation.sayThisLine: Drop, advance, cross, ready, control.

payload.prompt: Why is the transition zone called 'no-man's-land'?

options.text: Because you're caught in mid-court, neither at the net nor at the baseline, vulnerable to hard shots
Because no one plays in that area
Because the ball isn't allowed there
Because it's too far to run

explanation.correct: Mid-court is risky; you're too far from the net to volley and too close to retreat to the baseline.
explanation.incorrect: The transition zone is dangerous because you're caught in the middle, vulnerable to attack.
explanation.sayThisLine: Transition zone: cross it quick, don't linger.

payload.prompt: Complete the transition zone concept.
payload.template: The transition zone is {{location}} and is dangerous because {{danger}}; a {{shot-type}} gives you time to cross it.

explanation.correct: The transition zone is mid-court, risky because you're caught. A soft drop gives time to cross it safely.
explanation.incorrect: Mid-court is risky; soft drops buy time to advance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft drop buys time to cross the transition zone.

payload.prompt: Partners move left together when the ball is on the left side. Is this correct?

scene.alt: Doubles scenario: ball on left side, both partners moving left.

choices.label: Yes, move together to cover the side
No, they should stay in place

explanation.correct: Partners move as a unit (side-by-side) to track the ball and maintain coverage.
explanation.incorrect: Moving together (side-by-side) is essential to avoid gaps and stay coordinated.
explanation.sayThisLine: Partners move as a unit to cover gaps.

payload.prompt: What is the main reason partners move together as a unit?

options.text: To avoid leaving gaps in coverage and to stay coordinated against the ball movement
Because it looks better
To go faster
Because the rules require it

explanation.correct: Moving together maintains court coverage; gaps are how opponents score.
explanation.incorrect: Coordinated movement keeps coverage tight and prevents opponents from finding openings.
explanation.sayThisLine: Move as a team to cover gaps together.

payload.prompt: The ball is dinking cross-court to your partner. You're at the kitchen line. Do you slide toward them or stay in place?

situation.narrative: Your partner is getting a cross-court dink. You're both at the kitchen line, but she's moving to her right to get it.

options.label: Slide right with her to stay connected and cover the middle
options.consequence: Correct. You move as a unit; as she goes right, you follow to keep the formation and maintain middle coverage.
considerations: The middle stays protected as you shift

options.label: Stay in place while she handles it
options.consequence: This creates a gap between you. If her shot is weak, you're not in position to volley or cover the middle.

payload.expertNote: In doubles, partners are a team; move together to keep coverage tight and the middle protected.

lessons.title: Down the middle
lessons.objective: Decide who takes the middle and how to call it.

payload.prompt: A ball comes down the middle between you and your partner. You both go for it without calling. Good?

scene.alt: Doubles scenario: ball comes down the middle between partners.

explanation.correct: Middle balls create confusion. Call 'mine' to claim it and avoid collisions.
explanation.incorrect: Without a call, both players go for it, risking collision or a missed ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: Middle ball: call 'mine' to claim it.

payload.prompt: A dink is floating down the middle. You have a forehand here; your partner has a backhand. Who should take it?

situation.narrative: The dink is right down the middle. Your forehand faces the center; her backhand does.

options.label: You take it; your forehand is stronger than her backhand
options.consequence: Correct. The rule is: 'forehand in the middle' — whoever has a forehand to center takes it.
considerations: Forehands are typically stronger than backhands
Taking your stronger shot gives your team an edge

options.label: Let her take it; you'll back her up
options.consequence: You pass up your stronger shot. On the middle, you want your best stroke.
considerations: The middle is high-value; use strength
Forehand in the middle is the rule
She can back you up instead

payload.expertNote: The rule is 'forehand in the middle': whoever has a forehand to center takes the ball.

statement.speaker: Partner Alex
statement.text: Did you call that ball? We both went for it and I thought you were taking it.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: My bad, I should have called 'mine' when it came down the middle.
You should have known I wanted it.
It's just a dink, don't worry about it.
I always take middle balls.

payload.translation: Middle-ball calls ('mine', 'yours') prevent collisions and confusion. A missed call is on you, not her.

followUps.line: Yeah, I should have called it. Next time I'll say 'mine' when I see it coming.
followUps.why: Takes responsibility and shows you understand the communication rule.

followUps.line: We need to call our middle balls so we both know who's taking it.
followUps.why: Establishes a team habit of clear communication.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Middle-ball calls are essential in doubles. A quick 'mine' or 'yours' keeps everyone safe and coordinated.

payload.prompt: What is the most important communication call in doubles?

options.text: Middle-ball calls ('mine' or 'yours') to avoid confusion and collisions
Yelling 'come to the net'
Singing to stay in rhythm
Saying the score out loud after every point

explanation.correct: Clear middle-ball calls prevent collisions and missed opportunities; communication is the glue of doubles.
explanation.incorrect: Communication about who takes the ball is crucial. 'Mine' and 'yours' keep the team on the same page.
explanation.sayThisLine: Communication: 'mine' or 'yours' on every ball.

payload.prompt: Tap the stacked position.

diagram.alt: Doubles court showing both partners on same side

explanation.correct: Stacking is both partners on the same side to position strengths and maintain advantage.
explanation.incorrect: Stacking means starting on the same side, not the standard split formation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stacking puts both players on one side for strength.

payload.prompt: Put the stacking and switching steps in order.

items.text: Start stacked: both partners on the right side
items.why: You're keeping both forehands on the right side to maintain your strength.

items.text: The ball goes to the left side
items.why: Your positioning is now challenged; you need to adjust.

items.text: Switch: one partner moves to the left side to cover
items.why: Switching keeps coverage tight even after stacking.

items.text: You now have one on each side again
items.why: The court is covered and you've kept your strength advantage through the rally.

explanation.correct: Stack at start, switch as the rally progresses to maintain coverage while keeping strengths aligned.
explanation.incorrect: Stacking is the start; switching is the in-rally adjustment to keep coverage.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack to start, switch to cover.

payload.prompt: Complete the stacking and switching concept.
payload.template: {{stacking-def}} puts both players on one side; {{switching-def}} moves them to cover the court as play happens.

explanation.correct: Stacking is the start (both on one side); switching is the in-rally adjustment to cover the court.
explanation.incorrect: Stack first, then switch as needed to cover the court.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stack for strength, switch for coverage.

payload.prompt: Why would a doubles team use stacking?

options.text: To keep both players' forehands (or strengths) on the same side for better control
To make the court bigger
Because it's easier to run
To confuse the opponents

explanation.correct: Stacking lets a team keep strong shots (forehands) aligned on one side, giving them an advantage.
explanation.incorrect: Stacking is about positioning strengths; it's a tactical choice to keep powerful shots in play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Stacking keeps strengths on the same side.

lessons.title: Poach and target
lessons.objective: Understand poaching and targeting the weaker side.

payload.prompt: Your partner is at the net on the right. A ball comes to the middle. Should you poach (cross over) to volley it?

situation.narrative: The ball is coming to the middle, between you and your partner. She's on the right, you're on the left.

facts.label: Opportunity
facts.value: A poach could finish the point

options.label: Poach: step across to volley it aggressively
options.consequence: A poach can end the rally if you're confident in timing. But if you miss, it's a gap.
considerations: A missed poach leaves your side open

options.label: Let her take it; she's closer
options.consequence: Best; she takes her shot and you back her up from your side.
considerations: Backing up is a solid strategy

payload.expertNote: Poaching is offensive but risky; use it when you're confident in the timing and have told your partner to expect it.

statement.speaker: Partner Jordan
statement.text: You totally poached my shot and missed. That cost us the point!

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: I'm sorry, I should have called it first before crossing over. Let's talk about poaching.
I was going for the win, don't be mad.
You should have been ready to back me up.
Poaching is always the right play.

payload.translation: Poaching is aggressive but needs communication. A miscommunicated poach creates gaps and frustration.

followUps.line: Yeah, poaching works when we talk about it first. Let me know if I'm going for the middle next time.
followUps.why: Shows you understand that communication makes poaching work.

followUps.line: We can use poaching as a surprise, but only if you know it's coming.
followUps.why: Reframes poaching as a team tactic that needs trust.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Poaching is a bold play that only works with communication and trust between partners.

payload.prompt: One opponent is strong at volleys; the other struggles on backhand. Target the weaker player's weakness?

scene.alt: Doubles scenario: choosing which opponent to target.

explanation.correct: Target the weaker side or weaker player; it's where they struggle most.
explanation.incorrect: Targeting weakness is the offensive strategy; hit to the opponent's backhand and weaker player.
explanation.sayThisLine: Target the weaker side and weaker player.

payload.prompt: What is the main goal of targeting the weak side in doubles?

options.text: To force the weaker player to hit their worse shot, creating an error or weak return
To be mean to the weaker player
To tire them out
To confuse the stronger player

explanation.correct: Targeting weakness forces errors; the weaker player's weaker side is where mistakes happen.
explanation.incorrect: Strategy means exploiting weakness to create errors, not being mean. It's smart, respectful play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Target weakness to create errors.
